entries.title: Car insurance company with history of consumer complaints to pay Illinois over $200,000
entries.summary: <p>First Chicago Insurance — a car insurer that's drawn attention for its high number of consumer complaints — and a related company have agreed to pay Illinois $201,750 and improve their claims handling practices, after state insurance examiners uncovered numerous irregularities.</p><p>First Chicago and United Security Insurance, both owned by Warrior Invictus Holding Co., sell nonstandard auto insurance policies to drivers who don't qualify for coverage with better-known insurers, often due to poor driving records or a history of crashes.</p><p>The Bedford Park-based companies signed a consent order with the Illinois Department of Insurance on July 13 in which they didn't admit fault but agreed to the forfeiture. The consent order was announced in an Aug. 13 letter from the department to the companies.</p><p>First Chicago was the most complained-about auto insurer in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/10/18/nonstandard-car-insurance-consumer-complaints-american-alliance-first-chicago-insurance-united-equitable-american-heartland" >2024 Chicago Sun-Times investigation</a>, with its clients as well as drivers who were hit by First Chicago-insured drivers filing complaints with the state's Department of Insurance.</p><p>The order resulted from a market conduct examination conducted by Illinois regulators last year, in which examiners looked at the companies' practices from March 2024 through February 2025 and complaints from September 2023 through February 2025.</p><p>They found delays in the claims handling process, improper cancellations of policies and a failure to return unearned premiums in a timely manner, among other issues.</p><p>First Chicago was the subject of a previous market conduct exam in 2017 that resulted in a consent order requiring them to pay the state $61,850 in 2018.</p><p>Patrick Hincks, outside corporate counsel for First Chicago, said Monday that the company is committing "significant financial resources" to customer service to improve the claims handling process.</p><p>"We are really focusing on that and have been for the past couple of years," Hincks said. "We take customer service very seriously."</p><p>McHenry County resident Stacie Barger waited 17 months to have First Chicago settle her claim, after a First Chicago-insured driver collided with her car, totaling Barger's vehicle and injuring Barger and her passenger.</p><p>Barger said Monday that she's still waiting for a settlement check that was promised on Aug. 10. The accident happened March 1, 2025.</p><p>Barger said she was told on Friday that the check was mailed to the wrong party but that a new check would be mailed in seven to 10 days.</p><p>The 2024 Sun-Times investigation found eight companies, all selling nonstandard insurance policies in Illinois, had amassed exponentially more complaints than more well-known insurance companies.</p><p>The companies accounted for 5.28% of the state's private passenger liability insurance market and 2.85% of the damage insurance — collision and comprehensive — market in 2023. But they drew 1,340 complaints, which was about 40% of the 3,370 complaints filed in 2023 against auto insurers in the state.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/11/insurance-home-auto-industry-nonstandard-millions-claims-unpaid-analysis" >Insurance industry makes millions each day claims go unpaid, analysis shows</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/10/18/nonstandard-car-insurance-consumer-complaints-american-alliance-first-chicago-insurance-united-equitable-american-heartland" >Illinois’ most complained-about car insurance companies and how consumers can protect themselves</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Stephanie Zimmermann

entries.title: Week 2 takeaways: Geneva's Bennett Konkey and Mount Carmel's receivers dazzle; Loyola's time to earn No. 1
entries.summary: <p>It was supposed to be the year of the quarterback in Illinois high school football, but so far the receivers are stealing the show.</p><p>Geneva receiver Bennett Konkey posted so many highlight plays <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/28/oswego-high-school-football-geneva-ihsa" >against Oswego on Friday</a> that it is difficult to decide which moment was the most impressive.</p><p>Konkey is one of the fastest players in Illinois high school football. He’s a state champion track star, and that burst was on display when he sped past half of Oswego’s defense for a 53-yard TD.</p><p>Konkey out-leaped Iowa State recruit Dontrell Young to grab a 38-yard TD and even threw a key pass, finding quarterback Ben Peterson on a two-point conversion late in the game.</p><p>Geneva lost to Oswego, but Konkey opened eyes for the second consecutive game. The Illinois recruit finished with 10 catches for 217 yards with four touchdown catches, all for 27 yards or more.</p><p>Konkey had 178 receiving yards, two touchdown catches and a kick return TD in the Vikings’ Week 1 win against Libertyville.</p><p>“We just competed with the second-best team in 8A last year,” Konkey said. “That shows something about us as a football team.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Bennett Konkey leaps and grabs a jump ball pass. That is a 38-yard TD for Geneva. <br><br>Totally wild one here. Oswego leads 44-42 with 2:40 left. <br><br>That is Konkey’s 4th TD. <a href="https://t.co/iqudPkZckS">pic.twitter.com/iqudPkZckS</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2093533150173348154?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>More receivers sparkling</h3><p>Quentin Burrell and Marshaun Thornton, Mount Carmel’s highly-regarded receiver duo, earned raves in Week 2 for their parts in dragging the Caravan back from a 30-0 deficit to beat St. Joseph Regional, N.J.</p><p>Burrell, a Michigan recruit, had seven catches for 85 yards and three touchdowns. Thornton caught a pair of touchdowns.</p><p>Thornton, a 6-2 junior, has offers from Auburn, Notre Dame, LSU, Miami and all the prominent Big Ten schools. He also punts for the Caravan and occasionally throws passes on trick plays.</p><p>“The sky is the limit for Thornton,” Mount Carmel coach Jordan Lynch said. “He can play every position on the field and be the best at it. And he plays hard. He takes scout team reps just to help out the team.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/08/30/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >Michael O’Brien’s Super 25 high school football rankings for Week 3</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The big-play ability of Burrell and Thornton has made a few Caravan quarterbacks look very good over the past few seasons. Mount Carmel quarterback Brady Cloherty threw seven touchdown passes on Friday, breaking the school record held by Jack Elliott, who did it twice in 2024 and Jack McBride, who managed it in 1968. It was Cloherty’s first start for the Caravan.</p><h3>Time to prove it</h3><p>Loyola ascended to No. 1 last week and held on to the ranking after beating Indianapolis Cathedral in Week 2. But the Ramblers have been out of the local spotlight overall.</p><p>That changes this week. Loyola hosts St. Rita and Brother Rice over the next two weeks.</p><p>Junior quarterback Matthew Lee was excellent against Cathedral, finishing 21 of 26 passing for 297 yards with three touchdowns and one interception.</p><p>Lee shared the job with Dom Maloney last season but appears to have taken it over fully this year. Maloney is still making a major contribution for the Ramblers. The senior now starts at safety. He had a long punt return and a key interception late in the game against Cathedral.</p><h3>Coaching milestones</h3><p>Wilmington knocked off Morrison 48-0 in Week 2 to give coach Jeff Reents his 300th career win. Reents is just the 10th coach in state history to reach that mark.</p><p>Maine South coach Dave Inserra picked up his 250th career win in the Hawks' win against Warren on Friday.<br></p>
entries.author: Michael O'Brien

entries.title: Sammy Sosa disfruta de su relación reconciliada con los Cubs
entries.summary: <p>La vida parece sonreírle a Sammy Sosa. Juega mucho al golf, viaja y está firmemente de nuevo en buenos términos con los Cubs.</p><p>“Es como un matrimonio: a veces en el matrimonio te enojas con tu esposa, pero vuelves y la amas”, dijo Sosa sobre su relación con los Cubs. “Dejas todo atrás y sigues adelante.</p><p>“Siento que la forma en que me trataron… me alegra que hayamos llegado a esa conclusión y nos hayamos quedado juntos y, en gran medida, puesto nuestras diferencias a un lado. Ahora mismo, estamos contentos”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-940000" name="module-940000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Durante 13 temporadas, Sosa y los Cubs fueron sinónimos. En 1993 se convirtió en el primer jugador del equipo en robar 30 bases y conectar 30 jonrones en la misma temporada. Saltó a la superestrella internacional en 1998 gracias a su carrera de cuadrangulares con Mark McGwire y llevó a los Cubs al comodín de la Liga Nacional, ganando el premio al MVP de la liga.</p><p>Cinco años después, Sosa conectó dos jonrones y bateó .308 contra los Marlins en la NLCS de 2003, quedándose a un juego de llegar a la Serie Mundial.</p><p>Luego todo se vino abajo al final de una tóxica temporada 2004, cuando Sosa se fue temprano del último juego del año. Sosa, en declive comparado a sus días de 60 jonrones y acosado por especulaciones sobre el uso de drogas para mejorar su rendimiento, fue cambiado a los Orioles en enero de 2005.</p><p>Las dos partes estuvieron distanciadas hasta diciembre de 2024, cuando Sosa emitió un comunicado para disculparse por errores pasados, aunque no especificó cuáles fueron. Aun así, él y la dirigencia de los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2024/12/20/aparente-reconciliacion-entre-la-leyenda-del-beisbol-sammy-sosa-y-los-duenos-de-los-cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs se reconciliaron</a>, Sosa fue invitado posteriormente a la Convención de los Cubs 2025 y fue incluido en el Salón de la Fama del equipo.</p><p>El sábado participó en la celebración del 150.º aniversario de los Cubs en la Liga Nacional. Presentado ante la multitud antes del juego junto con un grupo que incluía a los campeones de 2016 y a miembros del Salón de la Fama, Sosa recibió una de las ovaciones más fuertes.</p><p>“Estoy agradecido de estar entre algunas de las leyendas que jugaron antes que yo”, dijo Sosa. “Estoy contento por eso”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Indicted ex-Loretto Hospital exec primed to point to feds' wrongdoing if he can't cut a deal
entries.summary: <p>Indicted<b> </b>former<b> </b>Loretto<b> </b>Hospital<b> </b>Chief Financial Officer Anosh<b> </b>Ahmed<b> </b>will try to strike a deal with federal prosecutors<b> </b>now that he’s back in the United States — but he’ll again raise claims of prosecutorial misconduct<b> </b>if they can’t reach an agreement.</p><p>That’s what defense attorney Dan Webb<b> </b>told<b> </b>U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman when Ahmed made his second court appearance Monday<b> </b>since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/28/loretto-hospitals-indicted-former-cfo-is-in-federal-custody-in-chicago" target="_blank" >returning to Chicago</a>.</p><p>Coleman once said Ahmed<b> </b>would see no relief based on misconduct allegations against the feds until he was “arraigned, in-person, before this court.”<b> </b>That event finally occurred Monday, when Ahmed briefly appeared before Coleman and pleaded not guilty.</p><p>“Glad to see you here, in the flesh,” she told him.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/28/loretto-hospitals-indicted-former-cfo-is-in-federal-custody-in-chicago" >Loretto Hospital’s indicted former CFO back in Chicago, will remain in federal custody for now</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ahmed, 42, faces fraud charges that could put him away for the rest of his life. But for now, he’s agreed to remain in federal custody while his attorneys try to cut a deal.<b> </b>He’s being held in the downtown Metropolitan Correctional Center, records show.</p><p>If no deal is done, Webb said he’ll be seeking Ahmed’s release and will use claims of prosecutorial misconduct before a grand jury to challenge Ahmed’s indictment. They’re similar to the claims that derailed the failed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> case<b> </b>earlier this year.</p><p>“We are trying to resolve this case,” Webb told the judge. “And we’re going to try to resolve it reasonably quickly.”</p><p>Ahmed’s next court appearance is set for Oct. 14.</p><p>The former hospital executive is charged in two indictments<b> </b>with scamming millions out of Loretto<b> </b>and the federal government. Prosecutors have said he left Chicago<b> </b>for France and Dubai<b> </b>in August 2023, after becoming aware of the investigation against him.</p><p>His attorneys said his return to the United States<b> </b>was delayed because of “several significant family health issues.”<b> </b>He was arrested<b> </b>in Serbia<b> </b>in November.</p><p>The probe that led to his indictment dates back to 2021, when Block Club Chicago<b> </b>reported the hospital had shared COVID-19 vaccines<b> </b>with employees at Trump Tower, where Ahmed had a condo. The vaccines were just becoming available and were still rare.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/29/loretto-hospital-fraud-anosh-ahmed-broadview-six" >Indicted ex-Loretto exec’s return to U.S. could add to feds’ ‘Broadview 6' headaches</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ahmed agreed to be returned to the United States after claims of prosecutorial misconduct spread at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >permanently<b> </b>dropped<b> </b>charges</a><b> </b>against two<b> </b>of his co-defendants<b> </b>in June<b> </b>after Coleman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/10/hearing-in-loretto-hospital-case-could-address-claims-of-prosecutors-misconduct-if-feds-dont-drop-it" target="_blank" >threatened to hold a hearing</a>.</p><p>The feds have since worked to strike deals<b> </b>with Ahmed’s four other co-defendants. </p><p>The misconduct allegations revolve around Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg<b>, </b>and they first surfaced in the failed “Broadview Six” case against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters. Mecklenburg also once handled Ahmed’s prosecutions.</p><p>Mecklenburg is accused of three types of wrongdoing in the “Broadview Six” case: Excusing grand jurors who disagreed with the feds’ case,<b> </b>having conversations with grand jurors outside the grand jury room,<b> </b>and a forbidden practice known as “vouching.”</p><p>Vouching occurs when a prosecutor puts her personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges.</p><p>In the prosecution involving Ahmed, the allegations against Mecklenburg include treating the indictment as a foregone conclusion and making “inflammatory characterizations of the defendants, including name-calling and folk-wisdom metaphors.”</p><p>But the feds last week secured a new indictment against Ahmed, which could be used to diffuse claims of past wrongdoing.</p>

</div> </div><p>La misión de los agentes de inmigración era absolutamente clara: detectar a los criminales "peores de los peores" que vivían en Estados Unidos sin estatus legal.</p><p>Ese fue el mantra que los funcionarios federales repitieron durante los 68 días más intensos del “Operativo Midway Blitz", que comenzó hace casi un año, el 8 de septiembre. Cientos de agentes armados y enmascarados de todo el país salieron a las calles en y alrededor de Chicago, deteniendo a miles mientras las cámaras filmaban.</p><p>Pero un análisis del Chicago Sun-Times/WBEZ de los datos de la Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) muestra que el despliegue masivo de agentes de ICE y de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) para capturar y detener a miles de personas que denominaban "criminales inmigrantes ilegales" resultó menos eficaz en Chicago que los esfuerzos más discretos que habían llevado a cabo antes, durante la segunda administración de Trump, y desde entonces.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8e0000" name="module-8e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Mes a mes, según el análisis de los datos de detenidos, la</p><p>campaña del otoño pasado para expulsar a los "peores de los peores" fue más publicidad que realidad.</p><p>Los agentes federales tuvieron mayor éxito deteniendo a personas condenadas por asesinato, violación, otros delitos sexuales y agresiones graves en muchos meses antes y después del auge del "blitz" que durante éste, según muestra el análisis.</p><p>Y solo el 15% de los inmigrantes detenidos en el área de Chicago durante la campaña tenían una condena penal previa, una caída sostenida desde un máximo del 50% justo después de la inauguración presidencial.</p><p>Los operativos de alto perfil fueron particularmente efectivas en al menos un área: cuando un detenido tenía una condena previa por "delito de tránsito".</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">This criminal alien's rap sheet is longer than a CVS receipt. He was found and arrested in Chicago with an active protection order from a prior assault arrest. His prior convictions include driving on a suspended/revoked license, DUI, assault, and domestic battery. <a href="https://t.co/GLUmHqEGLY">pic.twitter.com/GLUmHqEGLY</a></p>— CBP (@CBP) <a href="https://x.com/CBP/status/1987905692863283605?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 10, 2025</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Los agentes federales también lograron gran éxito al detener a inmigrantes con una condena previa por conducir bajo los efectos del alcohol (DUI), un delito priorizado por el exuberante <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=12122025%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=12122025%20Morning%20Edition+CID_14194dceee40c1980c345381fce1370b&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Gregory%20Bovino%20is%20the%20star%20of%20Trumps%20deportation%20show%20%20we%20traced%20his%20roots&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >comandante de la Patrulla Fronteriza Greg Bovino</a>, quien tenía 12 años cuando su propio padre cumplió condena por chocar ebrio su automóvil y matar a una mujer de 26 años.</p><p>Los datos de detenidos en Chicago no especificaron si alguien murió o resultó herido en cada caso de DUI.</p><h3>‘No tiene sentido’</h3><p>Cuando Trump recuperó la Casa Blanca en enero de 2025, prometiendo deportar a millones de inmigrantes mediante una aplicación agresiva de la ley, lanzó su campaña principalmente en ciudades demócratas que no votaron por él, incluyendo Chicago.</p><p>Para el 8 de septiembre, y el inicio del Midway Blitz, su Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) dedicó su despliegue a una víctima de un choque fatal por DUI en el interior del estado causado por un hombre guatemalteco indocumentado. Huyó del choque del 19 de enero de 2025 que mató a Katie Abraham, de 20 años, de Glenview, y a Chloe Polzin, de 21 años, de Deerfield, y actualmente cumple una pena de 30 años de prisión.</p><p>"Este operativo apuntará a los peores de los peores criminales inmigrantes ilegales en Chicago”, dijo DHS en un comunicado de prensa. “Si vienes a nuestro país ilegalmente y violas nuestras leyes, te buscaremos, te arrestaremos, te deportaremos y no volverás jamás”.</p><p>Pero a medida que las detenciones en Chicago se dispararon, superando las 3,800 durante los 68 días de otoño, aproximadamente 8 de cada 10 personas retenidas en la instalación de procesamiento de ICE en Broadview o en otras ubicaciones de Chicago no tenían condena penal.</p><p>Seis de cada 10 tenían infracciones civiles de inmigración, como quedarse más tiempo del permitido por una visa; el resto enfrenta un cargo penal no especificado pendiente.</p><p>Un portavoz de DHS respondió a una solicitud de entrevista con una declaración escrita que no abordó los hallazgos específicos y atacó los datos en bruto de ICE recopilados por la organización sin fines de lucro Deportation Data Project, que fue la base del análisis, calificándolos de haber sido "seleccionados" selectivamente. La declaración también afirma que esas estadísticas contabilizan los delitos sólo en Estados Unidos y no toman en cuenta los de otros países.</p><p>“Desde el primer día, las fuerzas del orden de DHS han cumplido la promesa del presidente Trump al pueblo estadounidense de arrestar y deportar a criminales inmigrantes ilegales, incluidos asesinos, violadores, pederastas, miembros de pandillas y terroristas”, dice el comunicado. “Lo que hace que alguien sea objetivo de la aplicación de la ley migratoria es si está o no ilegalmente en Estados Unidos, punto.”</p><p>Esta aparente falta de focalización coincide con lo que el principal abogado de la Coalición por los Derechos de Inmigrantes y Refugiados de Illinois (ICIRR) presenció en las primeras líneas de los arrestos y la defensa legal en torno a Chicago.</p><p>En lugar de tocar puertas específicas, los oficiales de inmigración estaban inundando los lugares donde vivían o se reunían inmigrantes, afirmó Fred Tsao.</p><p>“Vimos a gente siendo agarrada en la calle, personas que trabajaban en jardinería, que conducían Ubers, que vendían tamales en la esquina o vendían flores”, comentó Tsao. “Los derriban, los agarran, los tiran al suelo y los golpean… Y bastantes de esas personas optaron por no impugnar sus casos de deportación, lo que significa que quedaron separados de sus familias”.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Agentes federales de inmigración detuvieron a un grupo de personas para preguntarles sobre su ciudadanía el 6 de noviembre de 2025, mientras el comandante Greg Bovino, de la Patrulla Fronteriza, encabezaba una caravana en el lado suroeste.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Sobre las condenas por DUI, Tsao dijo, “No quiero minimizar lo graves que son estas ofensas”. Pero añadió, “¿Es un arresto, una detención y una deportación proporcional a la gravedad del delito?”</p><p>Los hallazgos se basan en un análisis de los datos de ICE recopilados gracias a una demanda bajo la Ley de Libertad de Información (FOIA) presentada por <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/12/immigration-customs-enforcement-ice-arrests-detentions-deportation-trac" target="_blank" >el Deportation Data Project</a>, un colectivo dedicado a la transparencia en la aplicación de la ley migratoria. El Sun-Times y WBEZ examinaron las detenciones iniciales registradas en el área de Chicago y los arrestos realizados en la región metropolitana de Chicago de seis condados entre el 20 de enero de 2025 y el 5 de agosto de 2026.</p><p>Los datos anónimos de ICE enumeran el cargo más grave para cada inmigrante condenado por un delito, pero no ofrecen detalles sobre los cargos pendientes en el momento de la detención.</p><p>Algunos puntos destacados:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-ee521b94-a593-11f1-adfd-3970010487a4"><li>Los datos muestran que 11 personas con condenas por agresión sexual fueron detenidas en octubre, durante el apogeo de la campaña de deportación del otoño de 2025. Pero los agentes federales detuvieron a 18 inmigrantes con condenas por agresión sexual en menos tiempo, durante los últimos 11 días de enero tras la inauguración de Trump. Capturaron 12 más en marzo.</li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-ee521b95-a593-11f1-adfd-3970010487a4"><li>Durante las nueve semanas de la campaña de deportación del otoño pasado, los agentes federales ficharon a cinco asesinos convictos. Sin embargo, habían detenido el mismo número justo antes, en agosto de 2025, y otros seis en mayo del mismo año.</li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-ee521b96-a593-11f1-adfd-3970010487a4"><li>También detuvieron a cinco delincuentes sexuales condenados durante esas semanas en otoño —pero siete en febrero de 2025, seis en julio y cinco en mayo de 2026.</li></ul><p>La situación desconcertó a Esteban Salazar. El encargado de mantenimiento de un edificio en los suburbios ha sido víctima de un inmigrante indocumentado que fue acusado de apuntarle con un arma. Al mismo tiempo, está horrorizado porque parientes suyos de origen mexicano, inocentes, fueron detenidos en las calles del área el otoño pasado, retenidos y luego deportados.</p><p>Carlos Mavarez Viloria, un migrante venezolano, había sido arrestado varias veces por robo y posesión de crack antes de febrero de 2024, cuando sacó un arma que Salazar describió como una Beretta negra pulida dentro de una tienda 7-Eleven del centro.</p><p>El arma resultó ser un encendedor que imitaba a una pistola. Pero Salazar, padre de dos hijos y casado, se preparó para lo que podría ser real. Cuando Mavarez metió la mano en sus propios pantalones y se dirigió hacia Salazar en la parte trasera de la tienda, amenazando con dispararle, Salazar agarró su propia pistola con licencia.</p><p>“Así que cuando sacó un arma contra mí, yo ya estaba en la parte trasera de la tienda. Me la estaba apuntando. No sé si llegó a ver mi arma, pero salió corriendo”, dice Salazar.</p><p>Los registros judiciales del Condado de Cook muestran otros cargos contra Mavarez hasta mayo de 2026, con resultados mixtos.</p><p>“¿Por qué diablos no lo pusieron en el primer avión o autobús de regreso? El tío de mi esposa que estuvo aquí 20 años lo detuvieron. Es ridículo”, dice Salazar. "Es duro. Como mexicano, como latino, trato de entender lo que hace nuestro gobierno pero no tiene sentido".</p><h3>Cambios de estrategia que podrían explicar las tendencias de arrestos y detenciones el otoño pasado</h3><p>Entre los oficiales enviados al área de Chicago el otoño pasado, la mayoría procedentes de asignaciones de la Patrulla Fronteriza y de ICE en una docena de otros estados, la administración de Trump desató una avalancha de publicaciones en redes sociales, ensalzando los arrestos de los "peores de los peores".</p><p>“El Operativo Midway Blitz está haciendo que Illinois SEA SEGURO de nuevo. Las fuerzas del orden de DHS han realizado más de 1,500 arrestos en Illinois, incluyendo pederastas, miembros violentos de pandillas y ladrones armados”, publicó DHS en X a mediados de octubre.</p><p>Semanas después, desde la cuenta de X de la Patrulla Fronteriza: “¡Otro malo detenido! En Chicago, CBP aprehendió a este inmigrante ilegal búlgaro con antecedentes que incluyen: violencia doméstica, agresión agravada con arma mortal, violación, no registrarse como delincuente sexual. ¡Contentos de tenerlo fuera de las calles!”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Another bad guy busted! In Chicago, CBP apprehended this Bulgarian illegal alien with a rap sheet including: domestic battery, aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, rape, failure to register as a sex offender. Happy to have him off the streets! <a href="https://t.co/9c3SL0I8qV">pic.twitter.com/9c3SL0I8qV</a></p>— CBP (@CBP) <a href="https://x.com/CBP/status/1985806077573664781?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 4, 2025</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Un cambio en los métodos de arresto en Illinois puede ayudar a explicar las tasas reales bajas de detención de inmigrantes con antecedentes penales graves.</p><p>Los agentes federales comenzaron el 2025 persiguiendo arrestos de inmigrantes indocumentados mediante 15 métodos de aplicación gubernamental. Pero entre septiembre y noviembre de 2025, registraron solo cuatro métodos.</p><p>Durante esos meses, no reportaron arrestos en virtud del Criminal Alien Program, que rastrea cuando los inmigrantes encarcelados terminan sus sentencias penales. Los arrestos por CAP habían representado alrededor del 10% de los arrestos entre enero y septiembre antes de que comenzara el Blitz.</p><p>Luego, del 8 de septiembre al 14 de noviembre, el porcentaje de arrestos definidos como "colaterales" superó a los "dirigidos" —53% frente a 46%. Así que más personas eran detenidas de forma aleatoria que intencional.</p><p>Pero del 15 de noviembre hasta marzo de 2026, mucho después de que la mayoría de los agentes federales adicionales hubieran dejado Chicago, los arrestos dirigidos eclipsaron a los colaterales, 72% frente a 13% (no se especificó el método de arresto para el resto).</p><p>Meses antes de que el Operativo Midway Blitz asaltara Chicago, el nuevo "zar fronterizo" de Trump Tom Homan se plantó en Portage Park en diciembre de 2024, prometiendo convertir a Chicago en el epicentro de las deportaciones. Un mes después, el Dr. Phil de la televisión acompañó a agentes de ICE en Chicago, interrogando a detenidos frente a las cámaras.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-244e33" name="image-244e33"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c7dbb20/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+317/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F11%2F811d80604248bdab4423c0ca88a9%2Ficeshooting-100525-09-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c90a27/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+317/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F11%2F811d80604248bdab4423c0ca88a9%2Ficeshooting-100525-09-2.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bada6e9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+317/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F11%2F811d80604248bdab4423c0ca88a9%2Ficeshooting-100525-09-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Agentes federales inmovilizan a un manifestante en Brighton Park, en el lado suroeste, el 4 de octubre de 2025. entries.title: Trump administration announces trucking school crackdown
entries.summary: <p>Two downstate federal prosecutors’ offices joined the U.S. Justice Department Monday in announcing a crackdown on trucking schools that the Trump administration claims has helped immigrants without documentation obtain commercial driver’s licenses.</p><p>Federal authorities shut down 110 CDL schools nationwide associated with more than 5,000 drivers “who failed English language proficiency tests,” according to the DOJ.</p><p>Another 160 schools were closed after inspections found inadequate facilities and some unlicensed instructors.</p><p>It wasn’t clear how many were based in Illinois. But the offices of two U.S. Attorneys from Illinois — Steven Weinhoeft of the Southern District and Greg Gilmore of the Central District — were named to a sprawling task force charged with auditing additional schools.</p><p>The federal government sets CDL testing standards while states issue licenses. A spokesman for Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias said their office follows national regulations and didn’t have any comment on the new initiative.</p><p>A spokesperson for Gov. JB Pritzker, a vocal Trump critic, said the administration was "choosing to attack truckers for how they look or speak."</p><p>"The Trump Administration is using veiled excuses to invalidate hundreds of training schools that doesn’t make our roads safer — they’re only attacking our critical trucker workforce and supply chains as our nation faces national truck driver shortages," according to Pritzker's office.</p><p>CDL holders and applicants are required to “show proof of legal presence and domicile” under federal law.</p><p>In Illinois, tests are administered only in English, a provision spurred almost three decades ago following a license-for-bribes scandal that contributed to the downfall of the late, federally convicted ex-Illinois Gov. George Ryan.</p><p>The federal task force comes on the heels of an effort by the Trump administration to gain access to databases with the sensitive information on thousands of CDL holders nationwide, a measure that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/13/illinois-sues-trump-admin-over-its-demands-for-cdl-database-information" >Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul has sued to block</a> along with the top legal officers from 20 other states.</p><p>The administration has threatened to cut more than $10 million in federal funding to the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators for not handing over the last five years of data from the Commercial Driver’s License Information System. The database was created in the late 1980s to help states determine driver eligibility for CDLs across state lines.</p><p>Raoul and other attorneys general claim the Trump administration is violating both state and federal law by creating its own version of the database without guardrails for the handling of sensitive information, such as Social Security numbers.</p><p>The lawsuits claim the administration “has no legitimate need to take over this database of state records, and it failed to consult the states before making this drastic change.”</p>

entries.title: Man killed in Chicago's largest mass shooting of 2026 was 'an outgoing person' who 'loved everybody'
entries.summary: <p>Like many former residents of the Robert Taylor Homes, Rontonio Guterz stayed connected through picnics near the site of the now-demolished public housing complex.</p><p>Though their childhood was rough at times, Guterz’s sister said the occasional reunions had become a point of pride.</p><p>“It's just bringing back that unity we feel like we missed out on,” Donna Guterz told the Sun-Times. “Our home was taken away from us."</p><p>On Saturday night, a celebration in Washington Park ended in tragedy when masked gunmen reportedly opened fire, killing the 35-year-old Guterz and wounding 14 others in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/30/mass-shooting-kills-1-injures-9-large-gathering-washington-park" target="_blank" >the largest mass shooting in Chicago</a> this year.</p><p>Donna Guterz is now planning her youngest sibling’s funeral — a somber event that will likely bring some of the same people back together.</p><p>"It's been terrible, just knowing the type of person he was," she said. "The outpouring on social media has been amazing. I didn't know my brother was that loved."</p><p>Local Ald. Jeanette Taylor (20th) said the attack had nothing to do with the reunion, which was wrapping up when the gunfire erupted. She called on those who know anything about the gunmen to step forward.</p><p>Meanwhile, Mayor Brandon Johnson said he was working closely with the Chicago Police Department “to hold those responsible accountable and keep our communities safe.” But, as of Monday evening, no arrests had been reported.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-680000" name="image-680000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ff04080/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6875x3858+0+364/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F85%2F07%2F8b263a694b69bf2f0b100048bf9e%2Fjohnson-260805-009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/014cbca/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6875x3858+0+364/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F85%2F07%2F8b263a694b69bf2f0b100048bf9e%2Fjohnson-260805-009.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6bf21fe/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6875x3858+0+364/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F85%2F07%2F8b263a694b69bf2f0b100048bf9e%2Fjohnson-260805-009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Mayor Brandon Johnson holds a press briefing at City Hall in the Loop, Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026. Dozens of shell casings were recovered, along with a weapon.</p><p>Rontonio Guterz was shot six times and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he died, according to the police report and the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>He was the youngest of 12 siblings and was known among family as "Tray," according to his sister, who said their life was challenging after their parents died a few years apart in the early 2000s. "We raised ourselves," she said.</p><p>Rontonio Guterz had a girlfriend and three young daughters, and he’d just bought a truck after earning his commercial driver's license, Donna Guterz said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a50000" name="image-a50000"></a> <picture In 2021, he pleaded guilty in a gun possession case and was sentenced to four years in prison, according to court records.</p><p>"Rontonio has made mistakes in the past," his sister said, "but he made up for them through the way he lived."</p><p>Over the years, the Robert Taylor Homes community stayed connected through their occasional picnics, though Donna Guterz said she had stopped attending them. Saturday's gathering was one of several they held this year, she said.</p><p>"Every year, they hang with each other. That's the one thing I do honor about us. We are united at all times," Donna Guterz said of the former Robert Taylor residents.</p><p>She has launched a <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/honoring-rontonio-aka-tray-baby?attribution_id=sl:8d00062f-25ec-4897-8f91-b8d946144aee&lang=en_US&ts=1788137695&utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&utm_content=amp30-control&utm_medium=customer&utm_source=native_options" target="_blank" ><u>GoFundMe page </u></a>to help pay for her brother’s funeral services. So far, she has raised nearly half of the $6,500 goal.</p><p>"He was such an outgoing person,” said Donna Guterz. “He loved everybody."</p><p>The 14 other shooting victims ranged in age from 21 to 47 years old, police said.</p><p>Jeanette Moore, 45, said she was catching up with other former residents of the Robert Taylor Homes when she was shot. </p><p>“I didn’t see anything, I just heard entries.title: Next two weeks give Cubs opportunity to make NL Central push vs. Brewers, but wild-card fate in balance, too
entries.summary: <p>You’ve seen the schedule.</p><p>Over the next two weeks, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> finally get their chance to control something about the NL Central race, as opposed to sitting and watching the Brewers sprint away with yet another division title.</p><p>But have you seen the standings?</p><p>No, not the ones that had the Cubs eight games back of the Brewers when the two teams started their four-game series Monday night at Wrigley Field.</p><p>The ones that had the Cubs knotted with the Phillies for the NL’s top wild-card spot, with the Diamondbacks and Padres sniffing around, too.</p><p>It’s been a summerlong wonder whether the Cubs could chase down the Brewers, who are steaming toward a potential 100-win season and holding a vice grip on the division.</p><p>At the start of the regular season’s final month, a new question: Will the Cubs even be hosting a wild-card series?</p><p>Answer, from the skipper: It’s not a question at the forefront of this team’s collective mind.</p><p>“The Cubs and the guys in that room, they’ve got a lot to say about tonight, and they don’t got much to say about Sept. 17 right now. So we’re going to worry about tonight,” manager Craig Counsell said before Monday’s game. “Does everybody want to play at home as many games as we can? Absolutely. Are we going to shy away from a challenge on the road? Nope.</p><p>“That’s how we look at it, and that’s how every competitor looks at it.”</p><p>It’s not to predict some sort of collapse, though on Aug. 1, the Cubs had a healthy – if far from insurmountable – lead as the NL’s top dog in the wild-card standings.</p><p>But after dropping four of their last five series, things have tightened considerably for the North Siders.</p><p>Math is not exactly on their side when it comes to making a surge for the division crown.</p><p>“It’s going to be, obviously, tough,” righty pitcher Colin Rea said. “They’re not slowing down.”</p><p>But hey, these Cubs can still dream, can’t they?</p><p>“I want to play [a playoff series] at home for our fans. But really, I’d like to skip a round,” Counsell said, referencing the reward for being one of the NL’s top two division-winners. “That’s not great for the fans, but I’d like to skip a round.”</p><p>Barring a big statement over the next two weeks, we could once more be discussing why the Cubs can’t get past the Brewers.</p><p>But there’s some new fodder, at least outside the Cubs’ clubhouse: this team possibly getting knocked from its wild-card perch.</p><p>What’s been one of the best teams in baseball for much of the season is nowhere near falling apart. The Cubs still woke up Monday with the sixth best record in baseball and regularly look the part of title contenders.</p><p>“We’ve positioned ourselves, through 140 games. We’re in a good place, absolutely,” Counsell said. “We’ve got a lot of fun ahead of us. We’ve got a lot of good things ahead of us. We’ve got challenges ahead of us. But we’ve put ourselves in a really good position.”</p><p>But the idea of Wrigley Field sitting empty in the postseason’s opening days is a lot more realistic than it seemed not too long ago.</p><p>The Phillies keep finding ridiculous ways to win, like on Friday’s down-to-their-last-out grand slam.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">THESE PINCH HITS LOVE SOSA <a href="https://t.co/Pisn2j2o5i">pic.twitter.com/Pisn2j2o5i</a></p>— Philadelphia Phillies (@Phillies) <a href="https://x.com/Phillies/status/2093553447366778938?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>The Diamondbacks just took two of three from the Cubs last week.</p><p>The Cubs topped the Padres in last year’s wild-card round but came a loss away from elimination. Would things have gone differently had the Cubs not been playing hosts?</p><p>With things as tight as they are as September begins, they might find out.</p><p>“I’m thinking those [dog] days are over,” Rea said. “We’re still in a good spot, but we know we still need to bring the energy every day and we still need to take it one day at a time.</p><p>“[We need to] not dwell on the losses too much, because we’re going to lose games. So it’s not letting the losses beat us up, just continuing to trust and have faith in what got us here to put us in this position that we’re in now. Just keep believing in that, really.”</p>

entries.title: Training camp is over but the Bears have a lot to get done before Week 1
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ meeting room seems packed to Bears coach Ben Johnson, whether he’s speaking to 90 players or 69 of them.</p><p></p><p>“I honestly don’t even notice the fewer guys …” the Bears coach said last week. “The train just keeps rolling on.”</p><p></p><p>It will pull out of the station Tuesday when the Bears hold their first practice since they trimmed their roster from 90 to 53 players. Tuesday morning, they’ll make their 16-man practice squad official, signing many of the players who grinded through what Johnson called a “nice, healthy, long, camp.”</p><p></p><p>Camp is over, but there’s plenty of work left to do — and a lot of time to get it done. When the Bears ended their last official training camp practice on Thursday in Nashville, they marked 30 days since veterans reported — but still 16 days until their season opener Sept. 13.</p><p></p><p>Some of those days will be a league-mandated rest. The Bears will practice Tuesday through Thursday this week before breaking for Labor Day weekend. When they return, they’ll dive into preparation for Week 1.</p><p></p><p>Here’s what the Bears have to accomplish before they play the Panthers:</p><p></p><h3><b>Caleb must keep growing</b></h3><p></p><p>Johnson plans to spend this week focusing on situational work. For quarterback Caleb Williams, that means red zone work, two-minute drills and short-yardage plays. For a coach that believes his team becomes what he emphasizes, that’s an important insight into where the Bears think Williams needs to improve.</p><p></p><p>Williams will continue to focus on his accuracy — Johnson is demanding a 70% completion rate — as well as his footwork.</p><p></p><p>After getting off to slow starts last year, Williams has been cognizant of his own energy at the start of practices and games. The Bears were sloppy early in their joint practice against the Cincinnati, making pre-snap penalties that enraged Johnson. They were much better early on during the Nashville practice.</p><p></p><p>“Just working on execution, the flags …” Williams said. “It’s leading from the head of the snake down to the tail. When we come out with good energy and we come out and we’re executing and we’re not having penalties as first team, it trickles down to second team and third team and just having that energy. … We’ve got to be able to start like that throughout the year.”</p><p></p><p>Williams struggled in the second half of Thursday’s practice.</p><p></p><p>“We’ve got to come out [of halftime] better, obviously, than we did,” Williams said.</p><p></p><p>Williams’ growth doesn’t stop just because the games start, either.</p><p></p><p>“There is no end line here,” Johnson said.</p><p></p><h3><b>Answer lingering questions on D</b></h3><p>Who is the Bears’ starting safety opposite rookie Dillon Thieneman? Who’s going to start at defensive tackle after the team traded Gervon Dexter on Monday?</p><p>Will cornerbacks Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson be healthy enough to play Week 1 after leaving practice Thursday? Who will play slot corner: safety Cam Lewis, rookie Malik Muhammad or newcomer Clark Phillips?</p><p></p><p>Those are the types of questions that the favorite to win the NFC — and the team that knocked the Bears out of the playoffs last year — doesn’t have to answer. On Monday, the Rams pulled Aaron Donald out of retirement and added him to a roster that features, for the first time in NFL history, both the reigning Offensive and Defensive Players of the Year. Their defense is terrifying.</p><p></p><p>The Bears’ defense, meanwhile, has issues — if not outright holes — in half its starting spots. Both Johnson and Bears general manager Ryan Poles will be asked about them when they meet the media Tuesday. The truth is, the Bears might not know the answers to the above until they get closer to the Panthers game.</p><p></p><p>Bears coordinator Dennis Allen was quick to recognize that a league-high 33 turnovers last year papered over a defense that, after giving up the fourth-most yards in the league, needed to be remodeled. The Bears rebuilt the unit in his image, adding speed in safety Coby Bryant, linebacker Devin Bush and Thieneman. One, Bryant, is out for most of the season. The other two need to be part of the solution.</p><p></p><h3><b>Get healthy</b></h3><p></p><p>Bryant hurting his knee during the first padded practice cast a pall on the rest of training camp. For the next two weeks, it seemed like every practice featured a new, scary injury. Left tackle Braxton Jones hurt his knee Aug. 6. Receiver Luther Burden hurt his groin Aug. 8. Running back Kyle Monangai injured his knee Aug. 16. Defensive end Austin Booker hurt his groin Aug. 20.</p><p></p><p>And then there’s slot cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/30/bears-leave-cb-kyler-gordon-on-pup-list-to-start-season-ruling-him-out-for-first-4-games" target="_blank" >Kyler Gordon</a>, whose baffling offseason calf injury has kept him from practicing during camp — and will cost him a minimum of four games. His extended absence —and his head coach’s curt responses to an inquiry about it — is downright odd.</p><p></p><p>Tackle Ozzy Trapilo, whose patellar tendon injury could have been career-threatening, has practiced on a limited basis but is on a unique recovery timeline and is unlikely to play early in the season.</p><p></p><p>Of the group, only Jones returned to full practices — just in time to win the starting left tackle job. Burden is right behind after Johnson said he looked 100% during pregame workouts Saturday.</p><p></p><p>The rest have 12 days to get healthy after a training camp when the opposite often happened.</p>

entries.title: Cubs releasing a 17-part 'bite-sized' rom-com on TikTok
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Cubs want you to get romantic about baseball. </p><p>Cubs Productions, the team's in-house creative arm, developed a 17-part romantic comedy called “Nine Innings to Love." The entire scripted series, told over the course of one Cubs game, drops this Friday, Sept. 4, only on TikTok. </p><p>In a statement, a spokesperson for the Cubs said the series was inspired by the "very real phenomenon" of fans finding love in the ballpark's bleachers. The team hopes the rom-com converts young people into baseball fans. </p><p>"‘Nine Innings to Love’ celebrates the magic of a summertime Cubs game through a bite-sized, episodic format that’s built for Gen Z and millennial audiences," said Jen Martindale, Cubs vice president of marketing and communications, in the statement. "By blending a game of baseball with BookTok fandom and the vibes of a classic rom-com, we've created a story that could only unfold in the Budweiser Bleachers at Wrigley Field."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@cubs/video/7680196259822488846?is_from_webapp=1&sender_device=pc&web_id=7672843392803964430" target="_blank" >The trailer premiered</a> Monday morning on the team's TikTok. Directed by Adam Sobel, the series follows Ava (Veronica Garrubbo), an aspiring romance writer who is "like, BookTok royalty," but she's in a slump, according to the trailer. Ava — at the Cubs game with a friend for a "girls' day" — meets David (Sid Kutikkad), her seatmate in the bleachers who doesn't "believe in romance." </p><p>Ava decides to take it upon herself to be his "wingman" and "love coach" to find him a "summer fling" inside Wrigley before the game is over, according to the trailer. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@cubs/video/7680196259822488846" data-video-id="7680196259822488846" data-embed-from="oembed" style="max-width:605px; min-width:325px;"> <section> <a target="_blank" title="@cubs" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@cubs?refer=embed">@cubs</a> <p>For those who believe in a good love story. entries.title: Teen boy dies after falling 100 feet from abandoned structure in Joliet
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old boy died early Sunday after falling from an abandoned Joliet industrial building, authorities said. </p><p>The boy was with four friends exploring the building, an old rock quarry structure near Louise Ray Parkway and east of Collins Street, according to a statement from the Joliet Police Department. </p><p>Just before 1 a.m., Joliet officers were called to the structure. They found the boy, who appeared to have fallen 100 feet from an opening toward the top of the structure, according to police. </p><p>First responders attempted to revive the boy, but he was later pronounced dead at the scene. The four young friends he was with were questioned by officers and later released to their parents. </p>

entries.title: 7 hospitalized after driver hits CTA bus in West Garfield Park
entries.summary: <p>Seven people were injured Monday morning after a driver failed to stay in her lane and hit a CTA bus in West Garfield Park, Chicago police said. </p><p>The driver — a 46-year-old woman in a Toyota sedan — was traveling east in the 4400 block of West Harrison Street when she veered out of her lane and struck the bus around 10:50 a.m., according to police. </p><p>The woman and two other adults in the Toyota were taken in unknown condition to Stroger Hospital, police said. Four adults on the CTA bus were taken to Stroger and Mount Sinai hospitals in good condition. </p><p>The driver was issued a citation, according to police.</p>

entries.title: City sues South Chicago Chapel owners over alleged building code violations: ‘The stench was overwhelming’
entries.summary: <p>The city of Chicago is taking the owners of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice" >South Chicago Chapel</a> to court for a litany of alleged building code violations — including the failure to keep buildings “clean, sanitary, and safe” after the recent discovery of 56 decomposing bodies on the property.</p><p>“The stench was overwhelming and could be smelled outside the building,” the complaint, filed Friday in Cook County Circuit Court, states. “There were swarms of flies at / near / on these bodies. There were numerous rats at / near / on these bodies. This is an immensely unsanitary situation.”</p><p>The city is asking a judge to issue a fine of $11,500 per day for every day the violations are not corrected.<b> </b>It’s unclear whether that means the owners could be ordered to clean up an area that some community members want to see deemed a crime scene.</p><p>The complaint stops short of requesting a complete demolition or condemnation of the building, though a judge should order that outcome “if necessary,” the complaint reads.</p><p>The complaint names funeral home owners Clark and Johanna Morgan, two of their business entities and a business entity that previously owned the building. Acting on a tip in early August, a crew of city and state agencies searched the building to discover dozens of bodies in various states of decomposition and vermin infestation at the business, which was created in 2022.</p><p>The list of 23 alleged violations span from the gruesome, unsanitary conditions discovered in the search to more mundane failures that include not having a single fire alarm or carbon monoxide detector throughout the building, or a construction permit for renovations.</p><p>The city’s Buildings Department declined to comment on the litigation. Representatives for defendants named in the case did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The housing complaint isn’t likely to silence calls for criminal charges against the Morgans. A Texas woman has already launched a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/11/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-mishandled-class-action-lawsuit" >potential class-action lawsuit</a> against the South Deering funeral home.</p><p>Over the weekend, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/30/south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-funeral-home-vigil-families" >families demanding answers </a>about what happened and how the owners will be held accountable asked the city to secure the area against trespassers or anyone going inside, including the owners.</p><p>A bright orange sign ordered the building closed, but it was placed out of sight until family members moved it to the front door Sunday evening.</p><p>The complaint comes after years of apparent inaction by the Buildings Department at 2939 E. 95th St., where South Chicago Chapel operated.</p><p>City records show that, after years of annual, failed inspections at the property, the Buildings Department failed to inspect it for four years from 2022 to 2026, covering the entire time the Morgans ran their business there.</p><p>After city officials searched the funeral home, a Buildings Department employee listed out potential violations that should be “expedited and amended” as part of an existing case, perhaps referring to the new complaint, which had yet to be filed at the time.</p><p>Those potential violations listed in the report include "deplorable conditions; rodent infestation; fly infestation; inadequate ventilation; unsanitary conditions; and the construction of or use of the second floor without appropriate plans and permits."</p>
entries.author: Mariah Woelfel

entries.title: Chicago offering $10,000 grants to help support food access on South and West sides
entries.summary: <p>Small businesses and farmers markets can receive one-time grants through a new city program set up to expand food access. </p><p>The Neighborhood Market Grant Program will provide up to $10,000 to small businesses operating in areas with low food access, according to a Friday news release.</p><p>The program's announcement comes a month after the abrupt closure of seven <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" >Save A Lot grocery stores</a> on the city’s South and West sides. Save A Lot's operator, Yellow Banana, had a redevelopment agreement with the city to keep the locations open for 10 years.</p><p>"Access to fresh, healthy food should not depend on what neighborhood you live in," Johnson said in the news release. "The Neighborhood Market Grant Program puts resources directly behind the small businesses and market operators who are helping change that — strengthening local food systems, supporting neighborhood entrepreneurs and expanding access to fresh food across Chicago."</p><p>Eligible applicants include retail, food and beverage small-business owners and farmers market operators who have a store in “priority geographies,” according to the city. </p><p>Funds can be used for equipment purchases, market operations, marketing and outreach, and improvements to keep markets open year-round.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/sites/bacp-recovery-plan/home/neighborhoodmarketgrantprogram.html" target="_blank" >Applications</a> will be accepted through Sept. 25 until 5 p.m. Spanish-language applications will be available starting Wednesday.</p><p>The program is funded by the Chicago Road to Recovery Plan, and Allies for Community Business provided $450,000 toward the program for grant recipients.</p><p>Earlier this month, Johnson also announced another program to help improve food access following Save A Lot's closure. The city has a partnership with Lyft, United Way of Metro Chicago and 211 Metro Chicago to give older adults on the South and West sides up to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2026/august/senior-grocery-rides.html" target="_blank" >two $25 Lyft credits</a> to help get to grocery stores. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" >Save A Lot stores set to close Saturday after years of turmoil, recent CEO death threatens city-funded deal</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
